scenes.heading: Sharding
scenes.narration: Sharding partitions a dataset across many nodes so that each holds only a slice, letting storage and throughput grow horizontally beyond a single machine.

scenes.heading: Choosing a shard key
bullets: Pick a key with high cardinality and even access
Hash sharding spreads load but kills range scans
Range sharding keeps scans fast but risks hot spots
A bad key creates hot shards and skew
scenes.narration: The shard key is the single most important design choice. You want high cardinality and evenly distributed access so load spreads across shards. Hash sharding hashes the key to spread writes uniformly, but it scatters ranges so range scans become expensive. Range sharding keeps ordered scans fast but can create hot spots when recent or popular keys cluster together. A poorly chosen key produces hot shards and skew that undermine the whole scheme.

scenes.heading: Hash vs range sharding

right.label: Range
points: Prone to hot spots on skew
Easy to split a busy range

scenes.narration: Hash sharding maps keys through a hash function so load spreads evenly across shards, but you lose the ability to answer range queries efficiently because adjacent keys land on different shards. Range sharding assigns contiguous key ranges to shards, which makes range and prefix scans efficient, but skewed or monotonically increasing keys create hot spots. Range schemes make it easy to split a busy range into two, while hash schemes often lean on consistent hashing to limit how many keys move during rebalancing.

scenes.heading: Consistent hashing to rebalance
steps: Map nodes onto a hash ring
Map each key onto the ring
Key belongs to next node clockwise
Add a node: only neighbors move
scenes.narration: Consistent hashing places both nodes and keys on a conceptual ring by hashing them. Each key is owned by the first node found clockwise from its position. When you add or remove a node, only the keys between it and its neighbor move, rather than reshuffling everything. Virtual nodes, where each physical node appears many times on the ring, smooth out the distribution and keep any single node from becoming a hot spot.

scenes.heading: The pain of cross-shard queries
bullets: Queries touching one shard stay fast
scenes.narration: Sharding is only free when a query can be answered from a single shard, which is why the shard key should align with your most common access pattern. Queries that span shards must scatter to many nodes and gather the results, which is slower and harder to scale. Joins and aggregations that cross shards are especially costly because data must move between nodes. And transactions that touch multiple shards require distributed coordination like two-phase commit, which is expensive and best avoided by design.

scenes.heading: Sharding plus replication
bullets: Replicas give the shard fault tolerance
Together they scale reads and writes
Sharding scales capacity, replication scales safety
scenes.narration: In practice sharding and replication work together. Each shard is not a single node but is itself replicated across several nodes. Those replicas give the shard fault tolerance, so losing one machine does not lose that slice of data. Combining the two lets you scale writes and storage horizontally through sharding while scaling read capacity and durability through replication. The mental model is simple: sharding scales capacity by splitting data, and replication scales safety and reads by copying it.

scenes.text: Sharding scales you past one machine, but the shard key decides your fate; design it around your real query and write patterns.
scenes.narration: Sharding lets you scale far beyond a single machine, but the shard key ultimately decides your performance, so design it deliberately around your real query and write patterns rather than choosing it by convenience.
